title: Module 4: Boundaries, Adverse Events & Ethical Decision-Making

questions.stem: A sonographer declines to discuss a patient's results with a coworker who is not involved in the patient's care. Which concept does this best illustrate?
options: Privacy
Implied consent
Circle of care
Confidentiality
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is the professional duty to protect information and share it only with authority; working in the same organization does not by itself give someone a reason to access information.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: For a cardiac echo appointment, who would generally be involved in the patient's circle of care?
options: A nurse who is not involved in the patient's care
An insurer requesting results without authorization
A relative waiting in the hallway, absent permission
The cardiologist who ordered and will review the echo
questions.explanation: The cardiologist who ordered and will review the echo has a clear care purpose; being nearby does not make someone part of this patient's care.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: Which documentation entry is most objective?
options: "Patient was anxious and uncooperative."
"Patient had a bad attitude."
"Patient reported feeling anxious, required two additional breaks to complete the study."
"Difficult study."
questions.explanation: The entry records the patient's own report and the objective facts rather than labeling the person.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: A sonographer says to a patient, "It'll just take a minute. Don't worry about it," without explaining what the echo involves. Which requirement of consent is most clearly missing?
options: Informed consent
Voluntary consent
Written consent
Substitute consent
questions.explanation: Without an explanation of what the examination involves, the consent is not informed — and an echo can take anywhere from thirty minutes to an hour.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: A patient says they are uncomfortable and asks to stop during an echo. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Finish the current view before stopping
Explain why the remaining images are needed, then continue
Document the concern and continue
Stop scanning and attend to the patient's comfort and safety
questions.explanation: Consent is ongoing — scanning stops immediately and comfort and safety are addressed.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: Which statement about consent forms is TRUE?
options: A signature automatically establishes informed consent
A form replaces the need for explanation
A form prevents the patient from withdrawing consent
A signature alone does not show that every requirement for valid consent has been met
questions.explanation: A form can record a decision, but it cannot replace the information and voluntary choice needed for that decision to be valid.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: A patient withdraws consent partway through an examination. What does this mean for the rest of the study?
options: The patient's agreement at the start stands and the study must be completed
Only a physician may accept the withdrawal
Consent must be re-established for anything further — the patient can withdraw at any time
Withdrawal applies only to written consent
questions.explanation: Consent continues throughout the examination, and a capable patient may refuse or withdraw at any time.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: Which action best reflects the duty of confidentiality in everyday practice?
options: Discussing the case wherever there is space
Leaving a workstation unlocked for convenience
Moving a care conversation away from the public area before discussing findings
Sharing a case in a private group chat
questions.explanation: Confidentiality applies whether information is spoken, written, displayed, or stored — so conversation location matters.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: A student removed the patient's name from an echo image before posting it, but the caption describes the patient's age, unit, and unusual finding. Why is this still a problem?
options: Removing a name cannot make information anonymous when other details may identify the patient — and authorization is still required
Private groups are exempt from privacy rules
Only names are identifying
Educational use is automatically permitted
questions.explanation: A combination of details may identify someone even after the name is removed, and de-identification is not authorization.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: Which documentation entry best distinguishes a patient report from an observation?
options: "The patient is dizzy and uncooperative."
"Patient reports dizziness when sitting up."
"Dizzy for no reason."
"Probably dehydrated."
questions.explanation: Attribution to the patient's own report separates it from the practitioner's direct observations.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: What must happen if you realize you accessed a record without an authorized purpose?
options: Delete the evidence and move on
Say nothing because no information was removed
Report it promptly through the organization's process — do not hide the event or alter records
Wait to see whether anyone notices
questions.explanation: Unauthorized access must be reported; concealment or alteration of records compounds the problem.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: Which combination best represents what "we bring from Part 1" into ethical practice?
options: Move quickly, document little, obtain a signature, and ignore refusals
Protect information, record facts, explain and respect consent, and remember that consent can be withdrawn
Share widely for teamwork, record opinions, and pressure gently
Diagnose independently and prescribe treatment
questions.explanation: Confidentiality, honest documentation, valid consent, and the patient's ongoing right to withdraw anchor the rest of the module.
tags: Review: Applying Privacy, Documentation and Consent

questions.stem: What is the CMRITO's stated position on sexual abuse of patients?
options: Case-by-case tolerance
Tolerance with an apology
Zero tolerance
No position exists
questions.explanation: The CMRITO has zero tolerance for sexual abuse of patients.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the legal definition of sexual abuse of a patient?
options: It covers only physical relations
It covers sexual physical relations, sexual touching, and sexual behaviour or remarks directed toward a patient, with an exception for what is clinically appropriate to the service
It covers only physical contact
It covers only conduct outside the workplace
questions.explanation: The definition includes relations, touching, and behaviour or remarks, except where the conduct is clinically appropriate to the service being provided.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Why does the definition of sexual abuse include remarks?
options: One sexual remark can change how safe a patient feels in the room, even without physical contact
Remarks are easier to prove than actions
Only remarks matter legally
Remarks are covered only outside clinical settings
questions.explanation: Words can cross a professional boundary even when no physical contact occurs.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: What is the "clinical exception" to the definition of sexual abuse?
options: Any touch a sonographer considers necessary is excluded
All clinical conduct is excluded
Only touch with consent is excluded
Touching, behaviour, or remarks that are clinically appropriate to the service are excluded
questions.explanation: The exception applies only to conduct that is clinically appropriate to the service provided.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: A sonographer touches a patient's chest during an echo without explaining why. Which statement is correct?
options: Any touch during an echo is automatically appropriate
Explanation is unnecessary for routine contact
Necessary clinical contact still requires clear purpose, explanation, consent, and respectful technique
Consent is unnecessary for clinical contact
questions.explanation: Calling something clinical does not automatically make it appropriate — purpose, explanation, consent, and technique all still apply.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which example is clinically appropriate contact in a cardiac echo?
options: A sonographer explains where the probe needs to go and why, and obtains agreement before placing it
Placing the probe anywhere without explanation
Contact the sonographer personally enjoys
Contact that the patient has not been told about
questions.explanation: Explaining the required contact and its purpose, then obtaining agreement, keeps necessary touch within professional boundaries.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: A patient becomes quiet and pulls their gown closed when the sonographer makes a sexual joke, and the sonographer replies, "Relax, I'm only joking." What is the most professional response from a student observing this?
options: Do not laugh along or treat the comment as harmless; support the patient, check whether they want to pause, and promptly involve the clinical supervisor through the appropriate process
Laugh to keep the atmosphere light
Say nothing because it was only a joke
Confront the sonographer loudly in front of the patient
questions.explanation: A sexual remark is not harmless; the patient's safety and the proper reporting process come first, with facts recorded — not speculation.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which statement about a sexual joke during an examination is correct?
options: Jokes reduce anxiety and are always acceptable
Jokes are acceptable if the patient laughs
A sexual joke is not a clinical explanation — explaining where the probe needs to go and why serves the examination
Jokes are acceptable if no one else hears
questions.explanation: Clinical communication serves the examination; sexual remarks do not, regardless of the patient's outward reaction.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: During an echo, a touch occurs that the patient does not understand. What is the best response?
options: Continue quickly to reduce awkwardness
Pause, ensure the patient is appropriately covered, clarify the purpose of the proposed contact, confirm permission, and seek the supervisor's guidance
Label the touch as appropriate because it was clinical
Ignore the patient's confusion
questions.explanation: Pausing to explain, cover, confirm permission, and seek guidance both respects the patient and clarifies the conduct.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: What is a useful sentence when a step of the examination needs to be clarified mid-scan?
options: "Hold still, this is normal."
"Don't worry about it."
"Let's pause so we can explain that step and check that you are comfortable."
"You'll understand later."
questions.explanation: The sentence pauses the procedure, explains, and checks comfort — the three elements of a safe clarification.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which statement about the patient's experience is TRUE?
options: A patient can have a technically good echo and still leave feeling unsafe
Technical quality guarantees the patient felt safe
Patient feelings are irrelevant to the examination
Safety feelings only matter if a complaint follows
questions.explanation: Professional conduct shapes how safe a patient feels, independently of image quality.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: What is the guiding principle stated for professional attention during an examination?
options: The patient should never have to wonder whether our attention is clinical or sexual
Patients should be told our personal opinions
Attention is a private matter for staff
Attention only matters during consent
questions.explanation: The clinical purpose of attention must always be clear to the patient.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which approach to explaining required exposure is most appropriate?
options: Promise that nothing will be uncomfortable
Explain the required exposure and positioning honestly, use appropriate draping, and check comfort throughout
Avoid all explanation to save time
Promise that the examination will take only a minute
questions.explanation: Honest explanation, draping, and ongoing comfort checks preserve dignity; an echo can take thirty minutes to an hour, so promises of speed and comfort must be avoided.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which statement about a quiet patient is correct?
options: Silence proves full understanding
Quiet patients never need explanation
Quiet patients should be scanned faster
A quiet patient may still have questions — check in if they look uncertain
questions.explanation: Quietness does not establish understanding or comfort; checking in protects both.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: What should be followed regarding chaperones and support?
options: The sonographer's personal preference only
The site's chaperone and support processes
The patient's family's preference only
No process — chaperones are never relevant
questions.explanation: Chaperone and support arrangements follow the site's established processes.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which statement about boundaries is correct?
options: Boundaries are unnecessary rules
Boundaries only apply to physicians
Boundaries protect both the patient and the practitioner and are part of safe care
Boundaries may be ignored when the patient is friendly
questions.explanation: Clear professional boundaries are a component of safe, trusting care.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: A sonographer uses excessive personal detail about their own life to comfort a patient. Which principle is at risk?
options: Empathy has boundaries — excessive personal disclosure can blur the professional relationship
Justice
Nonmaleficence only
Nothing — personal disclosure always helps
questions.explanation: Empathy notices emotion and responds without dismissing it, but it does not require excessive personal details or becoming the patient's counsellor.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which conduct would VIOLATE a professional boundary?
options: Making a sexually suggestive remark to a patient during positioning
Explaining the examination in plain language
Obtaining permission before contact
Offering a break during a long examination
questions.explanation: Sexically suggestive behaviour or remarks directed toward a patient fall within the legal definition of sexual abuse.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Why must students introduce themselves honestly as students?
options: Titles have no importance in consent
Only physicians need to be identified
Patients must understand who is doing what, and students must not claim credentials or abilities they do not have
Identification is required only for physicians
questions.explanation: Honest identification — "I'm a student working with your sonographer" — supports valid consent and professional integrity.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which student introduction script is most appropriate?
options: "I'm the cardiologist in training."
"Don't worry, I know what I'm doing."
"This will only take a minute."

"I'm a student working with your sonographer. We use a probe and gel on your chest to take pictures of your heart. We may ask you to change position. We'll keep you covered as much as possible. Please tell us if you need to pause or want us to stop."
questions.explanation: The script honestly identifies the student, explains the procedure in plain language, addresses draping, and invites the patient to control the pace.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which statement about a patient's control during the examination is TRUE?
options: The patient may only stop if a physician agrees
The patient's control begins only after the study is complete
The patient's control ends once the probe is placed
The patient may pause or stop at any time, and this should be stated when the examination begins
questions.explanation: Telling patients at the outset that they may pause or stop supports their autonomy throughout the examination.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: Which statement captures the relationship between clinical purpose and professional conduct?
options: Every action during the examination should be explainable by its clinical purpose
Clinical purpose is irrelevant to conduct
Conduct only matters when a complaint is made
Only the outcome matters, not the conduct
questions.explanation: If an action cannot be justified by its clinical purpose, it cannot be defended as professional conduct.
tags: Professional Boundaries and Sexual Abuse: Definitions and Practice

questions.stem: What is a reprimand?
options: A period of suspension
Removal of registration
A financial payment
A formal statement of disapproval
questions.explanation: A reprimand is a formal statement of professional disapproval recorded by the regulator.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: What does a suspension mean for a registrant?
options: The registrant practises with extra supervision only
The registrant's registration is permanently removed
The registrant cannot practise for a period of time
The registrant must pay a fine and continue practising
questions.explanation: A suspension prohibits practice for the specified period.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: What does revocation of registration mean?
options: The registrant is placed on probation
The registrant receives additional education
The registration is taken away
The registrant is reprimanded publicly
questions.explanation: Revocation removes the certificate of registration.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: Which statement about published discipline findings is correct?
options: Discipline findings are published
Discipline findings are always kept private
Only findings involving physicians are published
Publication requires the patient's consent
questions.explanation: Disciplinary findings are published as part of the regulator's public-protection function.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: Which statement about penalties for sexual abuse findings is correct?
options: Penalties are always discretionary
Penalties never apply to sexual abuse
Penalties are decided by the employer only
Some sexual abuse findings carry mandatory penalties
questions.explanation: Certain sexual abuse findings carry mandatory penalties under the legislation.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: After a professional conduct finding, which additional processes may follow?
options: No other process can ever follow
Separate employment or criminal processes may follow — one process does not automatically tell us the result of another
Only the criminal process may follow
Only the employment process may follow
questions.explanation: Regulatory, employment, and criminal processes are distinct; the outcome of one does not determine the others.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: What is the difference between an allegation and a finding?
options: They are identical
A finding is weaker than an allegation
An allegation is proven, a finding is not
An allegation is someone's account; a finding is a decision made after review
questions.explanation: An allegation has not been established; a finding results from formal review.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: Which statement about a charge and a finding of guilt is correct?
options: A charge automatically proves guilt
A finding of guilt precedes a charge
A charge is not a finding of guilt
Charges and findings are the same stage
questions.explanation: Being charged is an allegation proceeding through a process, not an established outcome.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the stages of the College's process?
options: Finding → complaint → referral
Referral → finding → complaint
Complaint → referral → finding, each a distinct stage
The three terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: A complaint, a referral, and a finding are different stages and should not be used interchangeably.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: At a discipline hearing, which statement is correct?
options: The patient is always the plaintiff
The College and the registrant are the parties; a complainant may be a witness; the panel considers the evidence before making findings
The employer decides the outcome
No evidence is considered
questions.explanation: The hearing structure has defined parties and an evidence-based decision by the panel.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: What is the College's overriding role?
options: To protect registrants from complaints
To increase departmental efficiency
To represent patients in court
To protect the public
questions.explanation: The regulator's decisions serve public protection.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: Which statement about the College's decision-making is correct?
options: The College reviews evidence, decides whether a concern should proceed, and makes decisions when a finding is established — it does not decide an outcome merely because a complaint was made
Every complaint automatically results in a finding
Findings are made without evidence review
The College decides outcomes based on public opinion
questions.explanation: The existence of a complaint does not itself establish anything; evidence and process determine the outcome.
tags: Findings, Consequences and the College's Process

questions.stem: What does "reasonable grounds to believe" mean in the reporting duty?
options: Absolute certainty is required
A vague feeling is sufficient
A criminal conviction is required
A reasonable person with the same information would conclude that the abuse likely occurred
questions.explanation: Reasonable grounds is a professional judgement based on the information available — not certainty.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: Which statement about the reporting judgement is correct?
options: It requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt
It requires a written legal opinion
It is not required until a complaint is filed
It is a professional judgement based on facts and observations, not certainty
questions.explanation: The duty is triggered by reasonable professional judgement, not by certainty or proof.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: Who has the legal duty to report suspected sexual abuse by a regulated professional?
options: Only hospital managers
Only patients
A registrant who obtains reasonable grounds during professional practice
Only police officers
questions.explanation: The reporting duty applies to registrants based on grounds obtained during professional practice.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: To whom must suspected sexual abuse by a regulated professional be reported?
options: The alleged professional's College
The local police service only
The employer's social committee
The patient's family
questions.explanation: The report goes to the regulator of the alleged professional.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: What is the usual deadline for reporting suspected sexual abuse?
options: 30 hours
30 weeks
30 days
There is no deadline
questions.explanation: The usual deadline for the registrant's report is 30 days.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: When must the report be made immediately instead of within 30 days?
options: When the report is convenient to make
When a lawyer approves the report
Only on weekdays
When there are reasonable grounds to believe the professional will continue abusing that patient or others, or that there is an urgent need for intervention
questions.explanation: Continuing risk or urgent need for intervention requires immediate reporting.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: What is required before the patient's NAME may be included in a sexual-abuse report?
options: Verbal permission from a relative
The patient's written consent
The alleged professional's agreement
Nothing — names may always be included
questions.explanation: Without the patient's written consent, the report is made without the patient's name.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: Which statement is correct about reporting without the patient's name?
options: Without a name, no report may be made
The duty ends if the name cannot be shared
Only named reports are valid
Not sharing the patient's name is different from making no report — a report is still required
questions.explanation: The duty is to report; the patient's name is included only with written consent.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: A patient asks the sonographer to promise not to tell anyone about the abuse they describe. What is the correct response?
options: Promise secrecy to gain the patient's trust
Explain that you cannot promise absolute secrecy, because there is a legal duty to use the applicable reporting process
Break the promise immediately without explanation
Ignore the disclosure
questions.explanation: You must use the applicable reporting process rather than promise absolute secrecy.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: Must a criminal conviction occur before the reporting duty applies?
options: Yes — only convicted professionals are reportable
No — do not wait for a criminal conviction
Yes — reporting requires charges to be laid
Yes — reporting requires a court date
questions.explanation: The duty arises on reasonable grounds; waiting for a conviction is not required.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: What is the consequence of failing to make a legally required report?
options: No consequence exists
Only an informal warning applies
Penalties apply only to patients
It can itself lead to penalties — reporting is part of professional responsibility, not an optional courtesy
questions.explanation: Failure to report a required matter carries its own professional and legal consequences.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: A student obtains reasonable grounds to believe a regulated professional has sexually abused a patient. What should the student do?
options: Make the registrant's report personally under the RHPA
Do nothing until graduation
Post about it in a study group
Promptly involve the clinical supervisor and obtain guidance — this differs from a registrant's personal legal duty
questions.explanation: The student's immediate step is supervisor involvement; the statutory duty applies to registrants.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: Which statement about gathering grounds is correct?
options: Record only conclusions
Investigate the colleague personally
Describe the facts and observations — do not draw legal conclusions
Gather opinions from other staff
questions.explanation: Facts and observations support the report; conclusions and personal investigations do not.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: What should a sonographer do if a colleague is the subject of the concern?
options: Conduct a private investigation first
Gossip with coworkers to gather information
Do not personally investigate; report through the applicable process and record facts and observations
Wait for the colleague to confess
questions.explanation: Investigation is not the reporter's role; the proper process handles the concern.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: A learner says, "I will tell a supervisor quietly and consider the matter handled." What is the best correction?
options: The learner is entirely correct
Telling a supervisor does not replace the personal duty where a legal duty applies — the applicable reporting process must be used
Supervisors handle everything automatically
Reporting is optional when a supervisor is told
questions.explanation: Supervisory notification does not discharge a personal legal reporting duty.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: Which statement about gossip is correct?
options: Gossip spreads awareness appropriately
Gossip substitutes for a formal report
Gossip protects the patient
Gossiping with coworkers does none of the protective things that reporting does
questions.explanation: Only the formal process protects the patient and triggers review.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: When more than one set of reporting rules may apply to one concern, what is correct?
options: Choose only one rule and ignore the rest
Wait until only one rule remains
Ask the patient which rule to use
Use the applicable reporting process for each duty — and seeking advice must not delay required reporting
questions.explanation: Multiple duties can coexist; each applicable process must be used without delaying a required report.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: Which set best summarizes the sexual-abuse reporting duty?
options: Anyone, any feeling, to the police, within one year
Registrant, reasonable grounds during practice, to the College, usually within 30 days — immediately if continuing risk or urgent intervention is indicated
Patients only, to the employer, within one week
Students only, to the school, within one semester
questions.explanation: The duty's who, threshold, recipient, and timelines match the first option.
tags: Reporting Suspected Sexual Abuse under the RHPA

questions.stem: What threshold triggers the child protection reporting duty?
options: Certainty that abuse occurred
A physician's written order
The child's request for a report
Reasonable grounds to suspect that a child under 16 needs protection
questions.explanation: The duty is triggered by reasonable grounds to suspect — you do not have to prove abuse before calling.

questions.stem: To whom must a child protection report be made?
options: A Children's Aid Society
The child's teacher
The patient's College
The employer's manager only
questions.explanation: Reports of suspected child protection needs go to a Children's Aid Society.

questions.stem: How quickly must a child protection report be made?
options: Within 30 days
Directly and immediately
At the end of the shift
After a supervisor approves
questions.explanation: Child protection reports are made directly and without delay.

questions.stem: A child discloses abuse during an echo. What should you say first?
options: "Are you sure that happened?"
"Thank you for telling me. I need to get help to keep you safe."
"I won't tell anyone."
"Let's find out together who is responsible."
questions.explanation: The response thanks the child, avoids leading questions, and signals that help will be sought.

questions.stem: When gathering information from a disclosing child, what must be avoided?
options: Listening calmly
Recording the child's own words
Suggesting answers or conducting your own investigation
Involving qualified help
questions.explanation: Interviews are conducted by qualified investigators; your role is to listen, record, and report.

questions.stem: How should a child's disclosure be documented?
options: Record the child's words accurately and describe relevant observations
Record your interpretation of events
Record only your conclusions
Do not record anything
questions.explanation: The child's own words and objective observations are what the record should contain.

questions.stem: What is the child protection duty for a 16- or 17-year-old?
options: No report should ever be made
Reporting is optional in all cases
The rule applies identically to all ages
The mandatory reporting rule does not apply in the same way, but a report should still be made
questions.explanation: For 16- and 17-year-olds the same mandatory rule does not apply, though making a report is still advised.

questions.stem: Who does the child protection duty apply to?
options: Only regulated professionals
Only people on shift
Everyone — it is a personal duty that also applies outside of work
Only hospital staff
questions.explanation: The duty is personal; you do not have to be on shift to have a responsibility to report.

questions.stem: What protection exists for a person who makes a child protection report?
options: No protection exists
The law protects the reporter unless they acted maliciously or without reasonable grounds
Protection applies only to physicians
Protection requires a lawyer's approval
questions.explanation: Reporting in good faith with reasonable grounds is legally protected.

questions.stem: Which statement about a child protection duty and a supervisor is correct?
options: Involving your supervisor is appropriate, but it does not hand over your personal duty
Telling a supervisor fully replaces the duty
Only supervisors may report
Reporting waits for the supervisor's decision
questions.explanation: Supervisor involvement supports you, but the personal duty to report remains.

questions.stem: How does the child protection duty differ from the sexual-abuse reporting duty under the RHPA?
options: They are identical duties
The RHPA duty applies to everyone; child protection applies only to registrants
Neither duty has defined recipients
Child protection applies to everyone and reports go to a Children's Aid Society; the RHPA duty applies to registrants and reports go to the alleged professional's College
questions.explanation: The two duties differ in who must report, the threshold, and the recipient agency.

questions.stem: You are unsure whether a situation meets the child protection threshold. What should you do?
options: Do nothing until you are certain
Wait for a colleague's opinion only
Assume the family will handle it
Contact a Children's Aid Society for guidance — do not let uncertainty delay a required report
questions.explanation: Guidance can be sought, but uncertainty is not a reason to delay reporting when grounds exist.

questions.stem: Which statement about proving abuse is correct?
options: You do not have to prove abuse before calling — reasonable grounds to suspect is the threshold
Proof beyond a reasonable doubt is required
A court decision is required first
A physician's certification is required first
questions.explanation: The reporting threshold is suspicion on reasonable grounds, not proof.

questions.stem: New information comes to light after an initial child protection report. What may be required?
options: Nothing further
Another report
Retraction of the first report
A written apology
questions.explanation: New information may require an additional report to the Children's Aid Society.

questions.stem: What is an adverse event?
options: Any event in a hospital
An event that results in harm connected with care
An event intercepted before reaching the patient
An event involving only paperwork
questions.explanation: An adverse event is one that results in harm connected with the care provided.

questions.stem: What is a near miss?
options: An event that could have caused harm but did not
An event that caused minor harm
An event that was never noticed
An event requiring no review
questions.explanation: A near miss could have caused harm but was intercepted or otherwise did not.

questions.stem: Which statement about reviewing events is correct?
options: Only adverse events are reviewed
Both adverse events and near misses may require review under workplace processes
Only events with lawsuits are reviewed
Near misses never require review
questions.explanation: Both categories reveal safety information and may require organizational review.

questions.stem: What is the FIRST priority after an adverse event?
options: Focus on the patient and their immediate needs
Complete the paperwork
Identify who is to blame
Notify the media
questions.explanation: Patient focus and immediate safety come first; documentation and reporting follow.

questions.stem: Which set best matches the steps after an adverse event?
options: Focus on the patient, notify the appropriate people, document honestly, and follow the organization's disclosure process
Blame, conceal, delay, deny
Ignore, resume, forget, repeat
Wait, wonder, worry, withhold
questions.explanation: These are the taught response steps for adverse events.

questions.stem: What must be avoided immediately after an event when facts are not yet known?
options: Notifying the supervisor
Inventing a cause or making promises before the facts are known
Documenting the observation
Providing patient care
questions.explanation: Speculation and unsupported promises undermine the disclosure process.

questions.stem: A student is involved in an event. What should they do promptly?
options: Manage the disclosure alone
Wait to see the outcome
Post about it for support
Contact their supervisor promptly
questions.explanation: Students promptly involve their supervisor rather than managing serious situations alone.

questions.stem: Why is a near miss still reported?
options: A patient avoiding injury does not erase a safety concern
Reporting near misses is optional
Near misses are only statistical events
Reporting near misses creates blame
questions.explanation: Near misses reveal problems that could harm someone in the future.

questions.stem: Which element is NOT one of the four elements of negligence?
options: A duty of care existed
The practitioner's personal opinion about the outcome
Care fell below the required standard
Harm occurred
questions.explanation: The four elements are duty of care, care below the required standard, harm, and causation.

questions.stem: What is the fourth element of negligence, after duty, standard, and harm?
options: The patient complained
A lawyer was retained
The breach caused the harm
The event was published
questions.explanation: Negligence requires a causal link between the breach and the harm.

questions.stem: What standard of care does negligence law use?
options: Perfection in every case
The practitioner's personal best
Zero mistakes ever
Reasonable professional care, not perfection
questions.explanation: The expected standard is reasonable professional care — not perfection.

questions.stem: Who evaluates the evidence in a negligence claim?
options: The employer alone
A court
The patient alone
The sonographer's classmates
questions.explanation: Negligence is a legal question evaluated by a court on the evidence.

questions.stem: Which statement about a poor outcome and negligence is correct?
options: A bad outcome always proves negligence
A bad outcome never involves negligence
Outcomes are irrelevant to negligence
A bad outcome alone does not answer the negligence question
questions.explanation: Outcomes alone do not establish duty, standard breach, or causation.

questions.stem: What is professional misconduct?
options: A legal finding made only by courts
An event that requires patient harm
A synonym for negligence
A professional conduct question — a professional rule can be broken even when no lawsuit follows
questions.explanation: Misconduct concerns professional rules and is distinct from the civil question of negligence.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates professional misconduct rather than negligence?
options: Making a reasonable clinical judgement that later proves imperfect
Asking a supervisor for help when uncertain
Deliberately changing a record to hide what happened
Reporting an error promptly
questions.explanation: Concealing an event through record alteration breaks a professional rule regardless of whether any lawsuit follows.

questions.stem: Which statement about waiting for a lawsuit is correct?
options: Only lawsuits trigger professional duties
Duties begin when a lawyer is involved
Nothing matters until a court decides
Professional responsibility does not wait for a patient to sue — you act on what you know now
questions.explanation: Professional duties — including correction and reporting — exist independently of litigation.

questions.stem: On review, you discover an incorrect measurement was entered. What is the correct moment to act?
options: Wait until someone else finds it
Quietly override the value without a trace
Delete the study
Discovering an error is the moment to speak up — honest correction follows the organization's process
questions.explanation: Timely, honest correction protects the record and the team's trust.

questions.stem: Why is quietly overriding information harmful?
options: It is inefficient
It undermines the record and team trust
It uses too much system storage
It is prohibited only in hospitals
questions.explanation: Untraceable overrides destroy the record's reliability and the team's confidence in it.

questions.stem: Which statement about documentation and safety is correct?
options: Good documentation excuses any unsafe practice
Good documentation cannot make an unsafe action safe after the fact
Documentation is the main safety measure
Documentation replaces corrective action
questions.explanation: Records describe what happened; they cannot convert unsafe practice into safe care.

questions.stem: A patient becomes dizzy moving off the echo bed and you prevent a fall. What should the record contain?
options: That the patient reported dizziness while moving off the bed, the assistance provided, and who you contacted
A blood pressure reading you did not take
A diagnosis of hypotension
Nothing, since no injury occurred
questions.explanation: Record what was reported and observed, the actions taken, and the contacts made — nothing invented.

questions.stem: A colleague says a fall was "just something that happens" while another says the practitioner "is definitely negligent." What is the correct approach?
options: Agree with the first colleague
Agree with the second colleague
Help the patient, obtain assistance, document, report as required, and let the appropriate review examine the facts — separating care from legal conclusions
Avoid documenting until fault is decided
questions.explanation: Care and documentation come first; the legal conclusion belongs to the appropriate review.

questions.stem: An echo appeared normal, but two days later the patient had new symptoms. Which statement is correct?
options: Nothing matters once the study is reported
Only litigation answers what happened
A clear record can help the team understand the facts, but it cannot make an unsafe practice acceptable — accountability means acting on what is known now
The interpreting physician alone is accountable
questions.explanation: Records support review, but accountability requires action on current knowledge rather than waiting for clarity.

questions.stem: A result was never communicated to anyone who could act. Whose responsibility is that?
options: No one's — the order was correct
Communication of a result that requires action is a shared professional responsibility through the approved process — it does not vanish because an order was correct
Only the scheduling clerk's
Only the patient's
questions.explanation: Correct ordering does not excuse failures in communicating results that need action.

questions.stem: Which set best matches the four contributions expected after an event?
options: Blame, denial, delay, concealment
Immediate care, review of what happened, response to the patient, and contribution to preventing recurrence
Silence, gossip, avoidance, forgetting
Lawsuit, insurance, media, resignation
questions.explanation: These four contributions form the professional response to an adverse event.

questions.stem: A patient asks what happened during an event. What is the correct approach?
options: Promise that nothing went wrong
Refuse to speak with the patient at all
Participate honestly in the disclosure process through the organization's process, without guessing about causes or blame
Blame a colleague
questions.explanation: Disclosure follows the organization's process with honesty and without speculation.

questions.stem: Which statement about the clinical record and the safety report after an event is correct?
options: The safety report replaces the clinical record
The clinical record replaces the safety report
Both are required and serve different purposes — one does not replace the other
Neither is required if no harm occurred
questions.explanation: Clinical documentation and organizational safety reporting are complementary obligations.

questions.stem: What is the safest response to an error you discover in your own work?
options: Correct it quietly and hope no one notices
Report it promptly through the correct process and participate honestly in the review
Wait to see whether it caused harm
Delete the evidence
questions.explanation: Prompt honest reporting is the professionally and legally safest course.

questions.stem: Which combination BEST reflects the module's approach to adverse events, negligence and misconduct?
options: Wait for certainty, hide errors, blame others, and respond only to lawsuits
Care for the patient, notify, document honestly, report and participate in review — remembering that a bad outcome alone proves nothing and that professional rules apply even without a lawsuit
Conclude negligence immediately whenever harm occurs
Assume misconduct only when a court decides
questions.explanation: The module teaches patient-focused response, honest process participation, and the distinction between outcomes, negligence, and professional rules.

questions.stem: What does professional liability insurance address?
options: Claims arising from professional practice, supporting the ability to compensate a patient when a covered claim requires it
Personal vehicle accidents
Equipment warranties only
Lost wages from missed shifts
questions.explanation: Professional liability insurance responds to claims arising from professional practice.

questions.stem: What may a professional liability policy pay?
options: Only marketing costs
The cost of defending a covered claim and the amount payable under a covered claim
Only equipment replacement
Only continuing education
questions.explanation: Coverage may include legal defence costs and the amount payable on a covered claim.

questions.stem: Who must hold professional liability coverage?
options: Practising CMRITO registrants, with coverage meeting the College's requirements
Only physicians
Only sonographers in private clinics
Only students on placement
questions.explanation: The CMRITO requires practising registrants to hold coverage that meets its requirements.

questions.stem: A colleague says, "My policy covers everything." What is the most accurate correction?
options: The colleague is correct
Only hospital work is ever covered
Coverage depends on seniority
The key word is covered — policies have terms, limits, and exclusions, so not every legal expense, allegation, or workplace is automatically covered
questions.explanation: Coverage must be checked against the specific work, workplace, and claim type.

questions.stem: A sonographer works weekdays at a hospital and takes shifts at an echo clinic. What is the correct understanding?
options: The hospital policy automatically covers both
No coverage is needed for the second workplace
Registration alone covers all workplaces
Coverage from one workplace may not cover a second workplace — verify the actual policy
questions.explanation: Multi-workplace practice requires explicit verification of coverage for each role and location.

questions.stem: What should a practitioner do regarding insurance BEFORE a claim occurs?
options: Wait until a claim occurs to read the policy
Assume the employer's policy is sufficient
Read the coverage, confirm the role, activities, and workplaces are included, understand claim reporting, keep the confirmation, and review whenever work changes
Purchase insurance only after retirement
questions.explanation: Insurance is something you confirm before a claim happens, and re-confirm whenever your work changes.

questions.stem: How should a practitioner verify their coverage?
options: By asking a colleague what they do
By assuming the brochure is accurate
With the employer or insurer, comparing the policy against the CMRITO's requirements, and keeping the confirmation
By checking only the price
questions.explanation: Verification includes checking the actual policy against regulator requirements and keeping written confirmation.

questions.stem: What must happen promptly if a claim arises?
options: Wait for the claimant to notify the insurer
Follow the notification process in the policy promptly
Ignore the notification requirement
Notify only if the claim becomes public
questions.explanation: Prompt notification is a condition of the coverage and supports an effective response.

questions.stem: Which statement about insurance and practice is correct?
options: Insurance authorizes any procedure
Insurance replaces competence
Insurance does not create clinical skill and does not replace authority, training, competence, or workplace arrangements
Insurance removes the duty to report errors
questions.explanation: Having insurance does not create a new clinical skill or any permission to practise.

questions.stem: Which pair of questions correctly frames coverage and practice?
options: "Is it busy?" and "Is it quick?"
"Did I sign the form?" and "Did I park correctly?"
"Am I authorised and competent to perform the task?" and "Do I have the required coverage for my practice?"
"Is it documented?" and "Is it popular?"
questions.explanation: Authority, competence, and coverage are separate questions that must each be answered.

questions.stem: When do students typically arrange their own professional liability coverage?
options: At registration, when they begin practising as registrants
On the first day of class
After their first claim
Never
questions.explanation: Students do not choose a product during the course — coverage is arranged at registration.

questions.stem: A sonographer says, "Insurance was purchased years ago and never reviewed." What is the problem?
options: Nothing — old policies are always valid
Only price matters
Coverage should be reviewed whenever the work changes — terms, limits, workplaces, and activities may no longer match
Only age matters
questions.explanation: Stale coverage can leave gaps; periodic review against current practice is required.

questions.stem: What is the correct question when an event occurs and coverage is uncertain?
options: Whether the event was serious
Whether anyone else was present
Whether the policy covers this work and this claim — not whether an event occurred
Whether the patient complains
questions.explanation: The existence of an event does not determine coverage; the policy's terms do.

questions.stem: Which statement about insurance and safe practice is TRUE?
options: Insurance makes safe practice unnecessary
Insurance authorizes work beyond competence
Insurance removes the responsibility to report errors
Insurance does not replace safe practice
questions.explanation: Coverage is a financial safety net — it neither replaces safe practice nor removes the duty to report.

questions.stem: What is an ethical issue in professional practice?
options: Any difficult technical manoeuvre
A choice involving more than one professional obligation, competing values, or uncertainty about the right action
Any disagreement about scheduling
Any equipment failure
questions.explanation: Ethical issues arise where obligations, values, or the right course of action compete or remain uncertain.

questions.stem: What is the FIRST step of the ethical decision-making process?
options: Choose the fastest option
Explain the problem in plain language
Document a conclusion immediately
Ask the patient to decide alone
questions.explanation: Plain-language framing makes the real problem clear before analysis begins.

questions.stem: What is the SECOND step?
options: Separate the facts from assumptions
Announce the decision
Avoid further questions
Transfer responsibility
questions.explanation: Facts must be distinguished from assumptions before any option is compared.

questions.stem: What is the THIRD step?
options: Ignore affected parties
Decide without input
End the discussion
Consider who is affected
questions.explanation: Identifying everyone affected — patient, team, and others — shapes the analysis.

questions.stem: What is the FOURTH step?
options: Select a favourite principle
Ignore the law
Ignore workplace policy
Identify the relevant principles and requirements
questions.explanation: The relevant ethical principles, law, and workplace process must be identified.

questions.stem: What is the FIFTH step?
options: Compare reasonable options and seek guidance if needed
Choose immediately without comparison
Refuse guidance
Act without considering options
questions.explanation: Reasonable options are compared, and guidance is sought when needed.

questions.stem: What is the SIXTH and final step?
options: Forget the matter once resolved
Keep the decision private
Delay documentation indefinitely
Document the decision and communication as required
questions.explanation: Documentation of the decision and communication completes the process.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly matches all six steps?
options: Explain the problem → separate facts from assumptions → consider who is affected → identify principles and requirements → compare options and seek guidance → document
Document → act → assume → forget → avoid → deny
Assume → guess → act → hide → delay → forget
Choose → act → explain → assume → conceal → ignore
questions.explanation: The full taught sequence is facts-framing, fact separation, affected parties, principles and requirements, options and guidance, documentation.

questions.stem: What is the correct status of this six-step framework?
options: It is a legislated six-step rule
It replaces professional judgement entirely
It applies only in court
It is a teaching framework for reasoning, not a quoted six-step rule from the CMRITO
questions.explanation: The framework supports reasoning; it is not a regulator-issued rule to be quoted.

questions.stem: Why must facts be separated from assumptions?
options: Assumptions are always correct
Assumptions can distort the problem; the facts determine what actions are defensible
Facts are less important than impressions
Separation delays care
questions.explanation: Decisions grounded in facts rather than assumptions are more accurate and defensible.

questions.stem: Which principle set is checked in step four?
options: Speed, efficiency, convenience, and profit
Respect for choice, honesty, fairness, and avoiding harm — along with the law and workplace process
Popularity, seniority, and tradition
Comfort, habit, and preference
questions.explanation: These principles, together with law and policy, form the requirements check.

questions.stem: When is seeking guidance the appropriate action?
options: When the right action is uncertain — guidance is a legitimate step in the process
Only after an adverse outcome
Never — guidance shows weakness
Only when a patient insists
questions.explanation: Uncertainty about the appropriate action makes guidance the correct next step.

questions.stem: Which statement about a technically correct action is TRUE?
options: Technical correctness eliminates all risk
Communication is unnecessary for technical actions
The patient's perspective is irrelevant
It can still create risk if it was not communicated, recorded, or considered with the patient's perspective
questions.explanation: How an action is communicated, recorded, and considered matters as much as the action itself.

questions.stem: What recurring thinking pattern supports ethical practice?
options: What is fastest? What is easiest? Who will notice?
What do I know? What needs protecting? Who can help me take the correct next step?
Who is senior? Who is popular? Who agrees?
What did we always do before?
questions.explanation: The pattern centers facts, protected interests, and appropriate help.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of learning an ethical reasoning process as a student?
options: You must handle every ethical situation alone after graduation
The process replaces the need for supervision
The process applies only to managers
You are learning a way to think, not being asked to manage a difficult situation alone
questions.explanation: The course teaches structured thinking and the appropriate use of support, not solo management of difficult situations.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures how ethical decision-making supports practice?
options: It removes uncertainty from every decision
It replaces law and policy
It makes reasoning transparent, connects the action to principles and requirements, and produces defensible documentation
It applies only after incidents
questions.explanation: Structured ethical reasoning makes decisions explainable, principled, and well documented.

questions.stem: A patient asks, "Is my heart okay?" before the report has been reviewed. What is the most appropriate response?
options: "I understand that you're worried. The cardiologist needs to review the study. Let me explain how you will receive the results."
"Everything looks fine."
"I can't tell you anything."
"Look at the screen and decide for yourself."
questions.explanation: The response acknowledges the worry, explains the review process, and avoids unsupported promises or dismissiveness.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: What is wrong with answering "Everything is fine" to a worried patient?
options: It is too brief
Nothing — it is kind
It promises a result before review, gives information the sonographer may not be authorized to provide, and may simply be wrong
It uses informal language
questions.explanation: False reassurance may feel kind in the moment, but it can damage trust, exceed the role, and be incorrect.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: What is the problem with the response "The doctor will tell you later"?
options: It is factually wrong
It shares unauthorized information
It makes a promise
It is technically true but dismissive — it fails to acknowledge the concern or explain the process
questions.explanation: Honesty without acknowledgement and explanation leaves the patient dismissed.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: Which three elements are required when a patient asks whether anything serious was found?
options: Diagnose, prescribe, and discharge
Acknowledge the concern, explain the review process, and ensure the patient's concern reaches the appropriate clinician
Promise, reassure, and hurry
Ignore, exit, and document nothing
questions.explanation: Acknowledgement, process explanation, and follow-through on the concern are the three required parts.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: During an examination you notice a finding that seems urgent. What should happen?
options: Wait for the routine report to be issued
Say nothing until the patient asks
Post the finding in a staff chat
Use the urgent finding communication process — waiting for the routine report is not a reason to delay an urgent concern
questions.explanation: Urgent findings move through the urgent communication process without waiting for routine reporting.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient says, "Just tell me it looks fine. I am not going to ask anyone else." What is the correct response?
options: Give reassurance because the patient insists
Explain that a diagnostic conclusion before physician review is outside the sonographer's role, and help the patient understand how results are delivered
Give a preliminary diagnosis
Agree to keep it a secret from the care team
questions.explanation: Patient insistence does not authorize diagnostic disclosure outside the approved process.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: What may a sonographer appropriately tell a patient about their examination?
options: A diagnostic conclusion regardless of authorization
Nothing at all, even about process
Whether the examination was completed or limited, and what needs to happen next
The interpretation before the physician reviews it
questions.explanation: Process information — completion status and next steps — is appropriate; diagnostic conclusions are not, unless authorized.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient complains that their previous record was incomplete. What should you do FIRST?
options: Review the documentation calmly before responding
Defend the previous sonographer immediately
Dismiss the complaint
Alter the record
questions.explanation: Checking the actual record precedes any response — defensiveness without facts is inappropriate.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: After reviewing an incomplete record, what is the correct course?
options: Hide the gap from everyone
Blame a colleague publicly
Rewrite the record secretly
Raise the concern through the proper process and respond calmly to the patient
questions.explanation: Concerns go through the proper process, and the patient receives a calm, honest response.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient hesitates after stopping and asks, "Will you be angry if I don't finish?" What is the best response?
options: "I'm not angry, we can stop, and I'll help you understand the options."
"We really should finish."
"The department will be upset."
"It's up to your family."
questions.explanation: The response removes pressure, is honest, and supports the patient's understanding of options.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: After a patient stops an examination, which set of actions is most complete?
options: Finish the current view, then discuss
Stop scanning, attend to comfort and safety, clarify concerns without pressure, involve the supervisor, and document what occurred
Pressure the patient, then document
Say nothing and reschedule silently
questions.explanation: The complete response covers stopping, comfort, clarification, supervision, and documentation.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient asks which medication will be started after their examination. What is the correct response?
options: Guess based on what you think the diagnosis is
Read the chart and prescribe verbally
Acknowledge the question and connect the patient to an authorized prescriber or care-team member who can answer it
Dismiss the question
questions.explanation: Treatment decisions belong to authorized prescribers; the sonographer connects the patient to the right person.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient asks when exactly they will receive their results. What is the correct approach?
options: Promise a specific hour
Explain the usual results process without promising a specific time you cannot control
Promise the results will be normal
Refuse to discuss the process
questions.explanation: Process explanation is appropriate; specific promises about timing you do not control are not.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: Which pair of responses should both be avoided when a patient presses for results?
options: Explaining the review process, and acknowledging the concern
False reassurance, and the abrupt "I can't tell you anything"
Directing the patient to the care team, and documenting the discussion
Checking understanding, and offering a break
questions.explanation: Both unsupported reassurance and abrupt refusal fail the patient — redirect helpfully instead.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: You identify an urgent concern about an inpatient during the echo. Who else should know?
options: The patient's nurse, in addition to the appropriate clinician, through approved communication
Only the patient's family
No one until the report is filed
Only the reception desk
questions.explanation: Inpatient concerns are communicated to the nurse and the responsible clinician promptly.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient says, "I'm scared something is wrong." Which response best reflects empathy?
options: "There's nothing to worry about."
"Don't be silly."
"I can see that you're worried. I will explain what I'm doing throughout, and I'll make sure the appropriate physician receives the study and that any concerns are passed on."
"That's not my department."
questions.explanation: The response notices the emotion, promises clear communication, and ensures concerns reach the physician.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: Which statement about false reassurance is correct?
options: It may feel kind in the moment, but it can damage trust, may give information we are not authorized to provide, and can be wrong
It is always appropriate for anxious patients
It is authorized when the scan looks normal
It reduces complaints
questions.explanation: False reassurance carries real risks to trust, role boundaries, and accuracy.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A family member in the hallway asks whether the examination found anything. What must you confirm first?
options: Whether the family member looks worried
Whether the family member drove the patient
Whether the hallway is private
Whether the patient has given permission or other lawful authority exists for that disclosure
questions.explanation: Privacy of location matters too, but the decisive check is authority to disclose.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient asks you to keep their results secret from their family. What is the correct approach?
options: Respect the patient's choice about who receives their information, within the limits of the authorized process
Promise absolute secrecy in every circumstance
Tell the family anyway because they are present
Ignore the request
questions.explanation: The capable patient controls who receives their information, subject to legal processes and duties.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: What should be documented when a patient ends an examination early?
options: Only "study incomplete"
The stop, the patient's expressed concern, what was completed, who was contacted, and the follow-up arrangement
Only the sonographer's opinion
Nothing until the patient complains
questions.explanation: A complete record supports continuity of care and any later review.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient asks whether a limited examination means they have disease. What is the correct answer?
options: An imaging limitation describes what could be obtained — it does not by itself diagnose a heart problem
Yes — limitations always mean disease
No — limitations always mean the heart is normal
Only the sonographer can diagnose from limited images
questions.explanation: Limitations concern image acquisition, not diagnosis.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient asks, "Are you a real doctor?" What is the most honest answer?
options: "Yes, I am."
"Close enough."
"I'm a cardiac sonographer — I perform the echocardiogram, and the physician reviews the study and makes the diagnostic interpretation."
"Why do you ask?"
questions.explanation: Honest identification of role and credentials is a professional obligation.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient declines recommended follow-up imaging. What is the correct response?
options: Pressure the patient until they agree
Tell the patient not to return
Respect the decision, explain the importance of follow-up within your role, involve the appropriate clinician, and document the discussion
Document nothing
questions.explanation: The decision is respected while information, escalation, and documentation are completed.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: Which statement about communicating during a long examination is TRUE?
options: Honest explanations of what will happen — without promising it will be quick or painless — support the patient's trust
Promises of speed and comfort are appropriate
Silence is best during long examinations
Patients never need updates
questions.explanation: An echo can take thirty minutes to an hour, so honest expectations are better than promises that may not be kept.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: A patient becomes anxious as the examination continues longer than expected. Which response best combines honesty and support?
options: Acknowledge the anxiety, explain what remains and why it matters, and check the patient's comfort
Continue silently to finish faster
Promise it will be over in a minute
Stop communicating entirely
questions.explanation: Acknowledgement, explanation, and comfort checks keep an anxious patient engaged and informed.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: What should you do when a patient's concern suggests something urgent?
options: Wait for the next clinic visit
Mention it only if the patient asks again
Handle it yourself alone
Ensure the concern reaches the appropriate clinician through the approved process without delay
questions.explanation: Urgent concerns must reach clinicians who can act, through approved channels.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: Which statement about the sonographer's communication role is correct?
options: Provide diagnoses whenever the patient seems ready
Refuse all communication about results
Communicate process and observations truthfully, acknowledge concerns, and route diagnostic questions through the authorized process
Promise outcomes to reduce anxiety
questions.explanation: Truthful process communication, acknowledgement, and authorized routing define the role.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: Which combination BEST represents a trustworthy response to a worried patient?
options: Reassure, promise, hurry, and forget
Diagnose, prescribe, discharge, and charge
Ignore, exit, and avoid documentation
Acknowledge the concern, explain the results process honestly, ensure the concern reaches the clinician, and document the discussion
questions.explanation: Trustworthy communication combines acknowledgement, honest process explanation, follow-through, and documentation.
tags: Applied Scenarios: Patient Trust and Communication

questions.stem: Another department is discussing a published regulatory finding, and details are confusing. What is your most appropriate role?
options: Add rumours to clarify
Stick to the published facts, avoid speculation, protect privacy, and redirect the discussion appropriately
Discuss the patient's private details
Announce a conclusion about guilt
questions.explanation: Professional discussion stays within published facts and protects privacy.

questions.stem: Which statement about published decisions is correct?
options: Publication makes patient details public property
Published cases may be discussed without limits
A published decision is not an invitation to discuss a patient's private information
Privacy ends once a finding is published
questions.explanation: The published decision does not remove the duty of confidentiality regarding patient information.

questions.stem: What is the College's overriding rule?
options: To protect the public
To protect registrants from complaints
To maximize departmental efficiency
To settle disputes informally only
questions.explanation: Public protection is the regulator's central purpose.

questions.stem: What does the College do before a concern proceeds?
options: Proceeds automatically with every concern
Reviews the evidence and decides whether the concern should proceed
Ignores evidence entirely
Defers every decision to the employer
questions.explanation: Evidence review determines whether a concern proceeds to a hearing.

questions.stem: Which statement about complaints and outcomes is correct?
options: Every complaint produces an outcome against the registrant
Outcomes are decided by public opinion
Complaints are findings
The College does not decide an outcome because a complaint was made
questions.explanation: Outcomes follow evidence and process — the existence of a complaint decides nothing.

questions.stem: In a discussion of a published case, what distinction must be maintained?
options: Between an allegation or charge and an established finding
Between weekday and weekend conduct
Between seniority levels
Between departments
questions.explanation: Allegations and charges are unproven; findings are established through review.

questions.stem: Which statement about other processes following a finding is correct?
options: Employment or criminal processes may also occur, and one process does not determine another's result
Only one process can ever apply
The regulatory outcome determines the criminal outcome
Employment consequences never follow
questions.explanation: Regulatory, employment, and criminal processes run independently.

questions.stem: A published finding involved a technologist accessing patient health information without consent or proper authorization. What is the professional lesson?
options: Access is acceptable if no information is shared
A password gives you access to a system, but it does not give you permission to read every chart
Authorization only matters for disclosure
Curiosity about someone you know is sufficient
questions.explanation: Technical access never substitutes for an authorized purpose — curiosity about someone you know is not enough.

questions.stem: What outcomes were included in that published finding?
options: A reprimand, required education, and payment of the College's costs
Automatic permanent revocation
No consequences
A verbal apology only
questions.explanation: The published decision included a reprimand, required education, and payment of College costs.

questions.stem: Which topics are appropriate in a professional discussion of a published case?
options: Patient safety, confidentiality, and the distinction between allegation and finding
The patient's identity and private details
Rumours about the registrant's character
Speculation about penalties
questions.explanation: Safety, confidentiality, and accurate terminology are the appropriate discussion boundaries.

questions.stem: What continues after a finding is published?
options: Nothing — responsibility ends with publication
Only curiosity
Professional responsibility — including confidentiality and respectful discussion
Only the appeal process
questions.explanation: Publication does not end the professional duties of those discussing the case.

questions.stem: A colleague mischaracterizes a published finding as a proven criminal conviction. What is the best correction?
options: Agree to avoid conflict
Add your own speculation
Clarify that a regulatory finding is a professional conduct decision, distinct from any criminal outcome
Leave the error unchallenged
questions.explanation: Accurate terminology protects both the registrant's fairness and the profession's standards.

questions.stem: Why should students focus on the professional responsibility in a published case rather than memorizing names and dates?
options: Names and dates are legally protected
Published cases are never examined
Responsibilities do not apply to students
The responsibility — such as authorized access to records — is what guides future practice
questions.explanation: The transferable lesson is the duty the case illustrates, not its identifying details.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST captures the professional approach to published findings?
options: Gossip about the details and speculate on guilt
Treat publication as permission to share patient information
Learn the responsibility the case illustrates, discuss it accurately and respectfully, and protect patient privacy throughout
Ignore published decisions entirely
questions.explanation: Published cases are learning tools, discussed within the bounds of accuracy, respect, and confidentiality.

questions.stem: Which set BEST matches the four main themes of this module?
options: Professional boundaries and sexual abuse, reporting duties, adverse events and negligence/misconduct, and professional liability insurance and ethical decision-making
Scheduling, billing, equipment, and marketing
Physics, instrumentation, anatomy, and physiology
Speed, volume, profit, and growth
questions.explanation: These four themes structure the module's content on ethics in practice.

questions.stem: A sonographer explains where the probe must be placed and why, obtains agreement, and uses respectful technique. Which themes are satisfied together?
options: Speed and efficiency only
Boundaries, consent, and patient dignity
Documentation and billing only
Equipment and image quality only
questions.explanation: Explanation, agreement, and respectful technique simultaneously serve boundaries, consent, and dignity.

questions.stem: You observe conduct that may cross a professional boundary. Which response integrates the module's teaching?
options: Support the patient, record facts and observations, involve the supervisor promptly through the appropriate process, and do not investigate or speculate
Investigate privately and confront the colleague
Gossip with coworkers first
Do nothing unless the patient complains
